synopsis: A plunge into Neptune's massive Great Dark Spot, navigating through turbulent methane cloud streaks.

shots.prompt:
One continuous 15-second first-person flight at 24 fps, filmed as if the camera itself is the spacecraft, moving forward without pause for the entire take. Seconds 0-4 are calm and wide: the real body fills one side of the frame, lit hard from the side, the far sun flaring at the frame edge, and the camera is already drifting forward. Seconds 4-6 accelerate toward the obstacle field and the first objects slide into frame. Seconds 6-13 race through the field itself: objects rush past on both sides and overhead, the nearest ones blurring, fine particles streaking past the lens, objects colliding and bursting apart, the body still showing through the gaps. Seconds 13-15 plunge into the densest part and the frame fills with the climax, the brightest and most overwhelming moment of the whole take, still moving forward as it ends. One continuous take, no cut, no fade, no scene change, and the camera never stops or hovers. Nothing of the vehicle is visible: no cockpit, no hull, no instruments, no HUD. No text, no captions, no logos, no watermark, no people. Sound: diegetic only and locked to what is on screen, a deep low rumble running under the whole flight, quiet and distant at the start, sharp impacts hitting exactly when objects collide, the whole sound field growing continuously and reaching its loudest and fullest in the final two seconds. No music, no voice, no narration.

A photoreal documentary flight into Neptune's Great Dark Spot, seen through a bare, disembodied camera: from the very first frame the image is open sky and Neptune edge to edge, sharp and fully unobstructed.

Seconds 0-4, calm and wide: the deep azure, finely banded disc of Neptune fills the left side of the frame, lit hard by the small distant sun from the upper right, black space above. Ahead lies the vast dark-blue oval of the Great Dark Spot, rimmed by bright white methane-ice clouds stretched into long crisp streaks by the wind. The camera is already drifting toward it.
Seconds 4-6: the camera accelerates and dips into the upper atmosphere; the first bright white cloud towers slide into frame, their sunlit tops sharp and detailed.
Seconds 6-13: the camera races through the storm's edge between towering white methane-ice cloud banks that rush past on both sides and overhead, the nearest ones motion-blurred, while dense swarms of glittering ice crystals and hail-sized methane ice pellets streak past the lens. Ice pellets strike each other and shatter into bright sparkling sprays. The dark blue vortex keeps showing through the gaps, its spiral bands clearly visible.
Seconds 13-15: the camera dives straight into the deepest dark-blue core of the vortex as sunlight breaks through a gap and lights a huge wall of swirling white ice cloud directly ahead, crisp and brilliant, the camera still speeding forward as the take ends.

Sound: diegetic only and locked to the picture, a deep low rumble of wind under the whole flight, quiet at the start, sharp cracking impacts exactly when ice pellets shatter, growing continuously to its loudest and fullest in the final two seconds.

caption:
This episode portrays a first-person flight into Neptune's Great Dark Spot, a massive anticyclonic storm comparable in size to Earth.

The obstacle field consists of extremely turbulent methane clouds, streaked with high-altitude cirrus-like white methane ice crystals. These clouds are driven by winds roaring at up to 2,400 kilometers per hour, creating immense pressure gradients.

The Voyager 2 spacecraft, during its 1989 flyby, provided the first and only close-up images of Neptune and its Great Dark Spot, revealing its dynamic atmosphere.

Such a flight is impossible due to the immense atmospheric pressure and crushing winds within the storm, which would instantly obliterate any spacecraft. The extreme cold, averaging around -218 Celsius, would also freeze most materials solid.

This is a simulation, not real footage. What do you think causes such colossal storms on gas giants?
